title: Fence the Sheep

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (convex hull by Andrew's monotone chain)

statement:
A shepherd has `n` sheep standing at points of a flat field (several sheep may stand at the same point). She wants the **shortest closed fence** that has every sheep inside or on it. Such a fence is the **convex hull** of the points: a convex polygon whose corners are some of the sheep.

A **fence post** is needed at every place where the fence **turns**; a sheep that stands in the middle of a straight stretch of fence does not need one. Report the number of posts and **twice the area** enclosed by the fence (this is always an integer).

If all sheep stand at one point, the answer is `1 0`; if they all stand on one line, the fence is a segment with `2` posts and area `0`.

**Input.** First line: `n`. Then `n` lines `x y`.

**Output.** Two integers: the number of fence posts and twice the enclosed area.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 20000 in this browser version (sorting dominates, so the idea scales to 10^6)
Twice the area can reach about 8·10^12; use 64-bit integers where the language needs it
hints: Sort the distinct points by x, then by y. The leftmost point and the rightmost point are certainly hull corners, and they split the hull into a lower chain and an upper chain.

Build the lower chain left to right with a stack: for each new point, while the last two stack points and the new point do not make a strict counter-clockwise turn (their cross product is zero or negative), pop the last point. Then push the new point. Popping on 'cross <= 0' also removes points that lie exactly on an edge.

Build the upper chain the same way going right to left, join the two chains without repeating their shared endpoints, and apply the shoelace formula to the corners to get twice the area. Handle the cases of one distinct point and of all-collinear points explicitly.
editorial: Use **Andrew's monotone chain**. Remove duplicate points and sort the rest lexicographically by `(x, y)`. Sweep left to right keeping a stack of the lower hull: for each point `p`, while the stack has at least two points `a, b` (the last two) and `cross(a, b, p) <= 0` (the turn `a -> b -> p` is clockwise or straight), pop `b`; then push `p`. The `<=` removes both interior points and points lying on an edge. Run the same sweep right to left to obtain the upper hull. The last point of each chain equals the first point of the other, so concatenate the chains dropping each chain's last point; the result lists the corners in counter-clockwise order, and its size is the number of posts. For one distinct point the chains degenerate, so answer `1 0`; for collinear points the chains each reduce to the two extreme points, giving 2 corners and area 0. Twice the area is `abs(sum over i of x_i * y_(i+1) - x_(i+1) * y_i)` (the shoelace formula, exact in integers). Sorting costs `O(n log n)` and each point is pushed and popped at most once per chain.

pts = sorted({(int(data[1 + 2 * i]), int(data[2 + 2 * i])) for i in range(n)})   # distinct points, sorted
